<!-- Thank you for sending your pull request. But first, have you included
unit tests, and is your code PEP8 conformant? [More details](https://github.com/freqtrade/freqtrade/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md)
-->
## Summary

Add custom_roi() strategy callback

## What's new?

This strategy callback introduces support for custom ROI logic, enabling users to define dynamic ROI thresholds based on trade side, trading pair, entry tag, indicator values, and more.

While similar behavior can be emulated using custom_exit(), there's no way to tell the backtest module what profit ratio you set for the exit, so it calculates the profit based on the candle's high/low, which often leads to inaccurate or overly optimistic results.

The new custom_roi() callback addresses this by returning a specific ROI value as a ratio. This integrates seamlessly with the minimal_roi logic used in backtesting, allowing for profit to be calculated using the provided threshold rather than arbitrary price extremes, resulting in more realistic and reliable metrics.

This improvement is also highly beneficial when using Hyperopt, as it enables more accurate evaluations and, in turn, better optimization outcomes.

discussion_timeline.author: xmatthias
discussion_timeline.body:
i don't really see the benefit over `custom_exit()` - not if you consider the implications / think it through properly.
As it's user controlled (while the trade is running), we can no longer rely on the user not using high, low or close to determine the returned value (by using data from `dp.*` methods apparently, as the method doesn't even get a current profit passed in).

As such - backtesting will have to treat it just like custom-stoploss (which is different to trailing-stoploss for backtesting, even though behavior can be similar / identical).
To me, this means - it has to become an explicit exit reason (not the same as one triggered by minimal_roi) - without the special calculation we can take for roi (as we control how it's calculated / determined).

Anything else will introduce a potential lookahead bias - one that's very difficult to spot at that - as (a user) will not think about this - and won't even be aware that this can cause a lookahead bias.


_to summarize_ - I'm not per se against the new callback - but it should not get the "special" minimal_roi treatment to avoid odd lookahead issues (at which point it's not necessarily a relevant callback any longer).

discussion_timeline.body:
I've never experienced lookahead issues in custom_exit. If you follow the documented way of accessing the analysed dataframe, there won't be issues.

The issue of backtesting accuracy with ROI and custom_exit is 100% down to historical data resolution. There's no single way to reliably ascertain when exactly an exit will happen based on the poor resolution data that exchanges provide as historical data, e.g. 1m at the finest scale.

discussion_timeline.author: mrpabloyeah
discussion_timeline.body:
> The issue of backtesting accuracy with ROI and custom_exit is 100% down to historical data resolution. There's no single way to reliably ascertain when exactly an exit will happen based on the poor resolution data that exchanges provide as historical data, e.g. 1m at the finest scale.

The inaccuracy issue only occurs in custom_exit; it does not occur in minimum_roi because it calculates the profit correctly.
In custom_exit, it is not possible to calculate the profit correctly because you cannot return the exit target as a ratio.

This callback allows you to set the exit target as a ratio, as minimal_roi does, and therefore the profit is calculated correctly, avoiding the inaccuracy issue that exists in custom_exit.

discussion_timeline.author: xmatthias
discussion_timeline.body:
> This callback allows you to set the exit target as a ratio, as minimal_roi does, and therefore the profit is calculated correctly, avoiding the inaccuracy issue that exists in custom_exit.

Well this is a whole different topic i think (one I'm not sure you should descend into 😆 )
there's no "inaccuraccy" with `custom_exit`. It's exiting based on either clearly defined pricing rules - or based on what the strategy returns as custom_exit_price.

Getting "exactly this rate" is a much more inaccurate approach if you think about it - as the exchange won't guarantee these prices - so if that's the reasoning - then this callback will increase inaccuraccy. 
While you THINK it makes it better, it really doesn't, and the only thing it'll benefit is overfitting ("i must use 2.955% as roi for BTC  instead of 3% or 2.9% - then profit is best" - whereas in reality - it's just overfitting to a minor price difference based on "high" - one you might never encounter in live (starting with the entry rate being a few ticks different, ...).

discussion_timeline.author: mrpabloyeah
discussion_timeline.body:
If you build exit logic with a 1% profit target, using custom_exit, you'll see in the backtest that the average profit is always higher than 1%; it could be 1.2% or 1.3%. Those results aren't realistic, and that's what I'm talking about.

However, if you build the same logic in custom_roi, in the backtest you'll see that the average profit is 1%, which is what you'd expect.

In both cases, the exchange doesn't guarantee those prices, but I think we can agree that the second case is closer to reality than the first, right?

discussion_timeline.author: xmatthias
discussion_timeline.body:
That depends on a case by case basis - and I'm not sure the new logic is better (it might look like that for your test case - but not necessarily for others)

if 1% is between low and open - it'll be what you're seeing.
If 1% is between open and high - your new results will be inflated - and previous average exits will be 0.8%. 

pessimistic is essentially always better in a backtesting scenario - results will be tuned to look inflated anyway (pure matter of fact - everyone looks for more profits, not less). 
Once slippage / market impact / ... hits - results will always pull you down a bit.


Just because you're using "roi=1%" will not guarantee that the actual exit happened at that rate anyway.
Backtesting might assume so - sure - but real markets won't do that - so a 0.2% deviation is WELL within what you can see on slippage - even on more liquid markets (not necessarily on BTC/USDT, but on most after XRP/USDT from a volume perspective) - at which point you're either into "use other side pricing / market orders" - or on the "risk not getting the exit" side - neither of which backtesting really covers.


As a matter of fact, you can get the same results with a combination of `custom_exit` with `custom_exit_price`.

---

If what you claim above is true - a 1% ROI exit (with the assumption that roi came into effect in this candle - which i think is what you changed it to now) should not exit at exactly 1% - but at the open rate (triggering the "came into effect" logic).

If it's not hitting that for whatever reason - then we'll need to look at this in more detail - as that's what I'd expect from what is returned by the new logic.

discussion_timeline.author: xmatthias
discussion_timeline.body:
I don't really like the way / approach this PR is taking (i can point out specific things - or rather did so for a few points above - but i think the overal picture will help more) - as i think it's trying making things WAY more complicated than they should be - slowly creeping towards something this PR really shouldn't even think of.

Let's focus in what we intend to improve here - and what the desired working is afterwards: 

**Currently** - the bot stops processing all signals (except timeouts and order adjustments) if there's an open order (entry or exit).
This creates a gap - where an unfortunately placed exit-order (one that doesn't fill and has a high timeout) can lead to extended losses - as it's "stuck" at selling for 60k - while price dropped to 40k - wiping our imaginary stoploss at 50k.

---

In my expectation of this PR (based on it's description and the discussion in the issue) - i'd assume this PR aims to fix this.

Essentially this means that the **future** state would be
* If no order is open for a trade - nothing changes, really.
* If an order is open / unfilled (entry or exit) - then the bot continues to process signals.
* If it encounters a new signal (keeping in line of the above 60k exit order - it encounters the stop signal at 50k)
  * it cancels the already open order _before_ placing a new order
  * it places the new exit order based on defined rules for this order

Now to complicate things (essentially a special case):
Between canceling the old order - and placing the new order - the trade "amount" may be updated (as the order partially filled) - so the new order needs to take this into account. That shouldn't really be a problem - as the trade will be recalculated uppon filling - just something to keep an eye on eventually.

So simplified the only thing that should change is:
* No check for `.has_open_orders` in most areas - as that's what prevents processing of the signals.
* added "cancel the open order if `.has_open_orders`" logic right before placing the new order (be that entry or exit).

This 2nd point is even there already (at least partially) uppon exiting - where a stop order will be canceled.

What this shouldn't touch is calculations - and i don't see where or why this part comes in (essentially most new properties).

discussion_timeline.author: Axel-CH
discussion_timeline.body: Thank you for the feedback, I will do the necessary changes.

discussion_timeline.author: xmatthias
discussion_timeline.body:
The _changed lines_ themselfs are ok - the problem is what's missing / not changed.
Behavior currently is kinda odd - with some callbacks being called independent of having an open orders - but with other callbacks (the most notable one being `adjust_trade_position()`) not being called.

This causes the following oddity:
Assuming my initial position filled - and the bot has an open, unfilled, position increase order - we'll still check for full exits (`custom_exit()` is called). 
It's however not going to check for position adjustments - so a partial exit would be missed / not called.

This invalidates base assumptions for the [execution logic](https://www.freqtrade.io/en/stable/bot-basics/#bot-execution-logic) - which are both very difficult to argue for - and are also oddly limiting for no real reason.

---

I think what we need (on top of what's currently changed)
* change behavior for `adjust_trade_position()` - allowing calls whenever in a position
* either ignore adjustments in the same direction - OR treat them as replacement order
* call `cancel_open_orders_of_trade` (from memory, the actual name is slightly different) from `execute_entry()` - so this scenario is also correctly handled.
* _[optional!] change behavior of force_enter to not check for open orders - but instead cancel existing orders (this one i'm not sure about yet_

discussion_timeline.author: xmatthias
discussion_timeline.body:
I like (mostly) how it behaves now (tested live for now - backtesting not yet) :+1: 

The only thing we need to have a 2nd thought about is how the `adjust_trade_position()` callback behaves.
It's clearly better now as it allows for a lot more flexibility in the strategy - what i didn't consider while writing the above however is that it'll lead to replacing an unfilled order on every iteration.

I constructed an example where the adjustment order would never fill - which led to the bot replacing the order every iteration.

only adding `if not trade.has_open_orders` to the condition stopped that behavior and moved it back to "regular" timeout behavior - so it's pretty clearly a breaking change to strategy behavior.

I don't necessarily mind that - we just need to be aware of it - and communicate it clearly in the release notes.

An alternative might be to have some graceperiod between "new order was opened and is still open" and "callback called again" - or a feature-flag which "keeps" old behavior - neither of which options I'm sure are a great idea.

Depending on this - we'll need to update the docs for this callback (it's now saying "This callback is not called when there is an open order (either buy or sell) waiting for execution." - which turns wrong now).

discussion_timeline.body:
What do you think about using the **order_tag** as a key to decide if we need to replace the order.
If you try create a new entry order with same order_tag, quantity and price the unfullfilled order won't be replaced.

discussion_timeline.author: xmatthias
discussion_timeline.body:
well where would an "order_tag" come from? (how will the bot automatically determine if the tag is the same or a different one?)
If you expect the strategy to return this:

## Summary

Some exchanges express their minimal amount in terms of contract, for example, if you run `node ccxt/examples/js/cli gateio fetchMarkets '{"type": "swap"}` you can see a field called `contractSize`, and for BTC this value is `0.0001`. This means that 1 contract of BTC is worth 0.0001 BTC, and the minimal order is for 1 contract. It makes more sense for us to handle all exchanges as ordering the amount of the underlying asset (this is how binance does it anyway). Also all prices are given in relation to the underlying asset anyway

issue_payload.body:
## Summary
Enables building app in a conda environment or Docker container using a Makefile

Solve the issue: #2041 

## Quick changelog

- Added Makefile
- Updated .dockerignore/.gitignore
- Created new logic for generation of startup files
- Added .env file to separate configuration from strategies
- Added support for version control of a repo located at `user_data/user_repo` so users can keep custom strategies, scripts, and jupyter notebooks backed up

## What's new?
This is a proposed alternative to the installation process intended to:

- Streamline the installation options
- Make working with Docker containers less cumbersome and
- Add support for installation in a conda environment. 

The existing `setup.sh` script is untouched and will continue to work as a parallel installation option.

### Configuration

- Overwrite configuration defaults by copying `.env.example` to `~/.freqtrade/.env`, `user_data/.env` or `user_data/user_repo.env`. 
- Execute `make` from the project root to view available commands
- Build conda app with `make conda-app`
- Build docker app with `make docker-app`

well there's 2 contradicting statements in this sentence to me - you're either a user - wanting an easy way to install - which hopefully is something around `pip install freqtrade` in the future,
OR you want it in your favorite development environment (because you're a developer) - so you'll have different requirements (like checking out code and such).
Also, as developer, you'll have personal preferences to install (me personally,i use pyenv), which you're familiar with - so either pip or conda could be wrong eventually, and satisfying everyone is not easily done in this regard (however being developers, everyone will have his own solutions).

**installation future**
we have problems with installation currently, most related to some dependencies (ta-lib, py_1st_find), which don't install easily, and others are the handling of user_data folders.
Once these problems are solved (or workarounds found), i expect to publish freqtrade to pypi, which will make installation as easy as `pip install freqtrade`.
Since users won't have any other files in this case (makefile, docker-compose file...) - which they would need to get through a different  method (probably from git) - that will make these options far less accessible, since it'll limit to the subsection of developers.


**regular users** 
For a regular user, the only "really" needed argument is `--config` - since every cli argument (argument, not comand!) can be added to the configuration file as well, so you'll only need `--config` (and mounts, in case of docker).

**docker**
for docker, using something like `alias dockerft=...` can be an option (so would `docker-compose.yml` be, where you can configure all mounts) - but honestly, I've not received complaints about the length of commands yet, so either everyone has his own method to handle this, or it's not a very common problem.

metadata.title: Parallelisation of iterative data downloads for speed improvement

issue_payload.body: ## Summary Speeds up iterative data downloading by introducing the option to use parallelisation, where it is possible in one request per pair, whilst retaining all existing functionality. Provides great speed improvements to iterative data downloading, typically 90%+ reduction in time to download pairs. Only applies when a timerange is a specified via days or timerange. Using Binance : `freqtrade download-data --pairs ".*/USDT" -t 5m 15m --days 2` Pre changes (takes 14:40 mins or 880 secs for 812 downloads): Post changes and using async parallelisation (takes 1:01 mins or 61 secs for 812 downloads): This one example provides an over 93% speed reduction to the iterative downloads - 61 / 880 = 6.9%, but this is typical for all pairs over a short period. ## Quick changelog - Introduces a new ohlcv collection method that uses the async parallel downloads to grab all pairs, where the requested data can be collected within one request per pair. - Requires a time range via timerange or days. - Works on all timeframes and candle types. - Both collection methods can still be used in the same script. For example : `freqtrade download-data --pairs ".*/USDT" -t 5m 15m --days 5` will use the parallel method for the 15m (as 4 * 24 * 5 < 1000), but default back to the old method for the 5m (as 12 * 24 * 5 < 1000). - Did not seem appropriate to do this for prepend or erase. Defaults to old method. - All previous functionality still works. ## What's new? As discussed in this question (https://github.com/freqtrade/freqtrade/issues/11624#issuecomment-2794341375) - "Current method of data downloading penalizes smallish downloads to some degree", so where the data can be downloaded in one request we try to take advantage of async parallelisation, whilst maintaining all the existing functionality where that is not appropriate. As per the docs: `The idea is to download a big chunk of data once, and then iteratively increase the amount of data stored.` A typical use case of this would be to download the candles for all pairs in a large chunk, and then run a daily cron job / download script to collect the latest days data for those pairs, and iteratively update. With a typical candle limit of 1000, one days worth of data for 5m/15m/30m/1h/4h/1d candles can all be downloaded in one request per pair, which lends itself much better to parallelisation, rather than the loop. ## Potential Improvements - If the double nested loop (see below) was timeframe -> pairs, rather than pairs -> timeframe, we could move the `_download_all_pairs_history_parallel` outside the inner loop and it would not require all the additional checking each innter loop ` ((pair, timeframe, candle_type) not in fast_candles)` (which is a proxy for have we already done this), and that would be better. But that was a larger change than I was prepared to make. https://github.com/freqtrade/freqtrade/blob/30eb32862c2574fb0235dfb99d34e7728a8c7462/freqtrade/data/history/history_utils.py#L349-L358

Keep in mind that accepting a PR _always_ means that i take responsibility for the code you add - with the (usually time-unconstraint) responsibility to maintain that code going forward.

It's a scheduled job - run it overnight, nobody will care how long it takes - so it's an edge-case improvement - which bears more risk than what it'll actually help.

You "consistency test" is really based on one thing - data is available up to "1" call ago (that consistency test shows the output - but not how it was archived. just because it's running in parallel doesn't make it better or worse - it'll depend on the previous state of the data.


What i mean is the following functionality (to avoid "gaps" in the data).
Even if you pass in `--days 1` - download-data might need to download weeks of data depending on existing data availability (i could schedule a job to run once a week to refresh my data - BUT - i could still pass `--days 1` - and it would still download the 5 days of missing data - as it loads the data, checks "how much historic data do i need" - and then starts the download based on that.

To know "1 call is enough" - you can't rely on `--days 1` was passed in - but you need to have loaded the data to know the previous end date.
If you do that - you'll have the data in memory. 

it's hence a trade-off - with either 
1. "you load the data and make sure you download what you need" 
1. "you take a guess and ignore that you'll cause gaps in the data" 
1. "you download the data regardless, and then throw it away if it doesn't match" (which is what i think you tried _based on your explanation_) -

Based on 3 -  you essentially invert the penalty from "we penalize short downloads" to "we penalize intermediate / long downloads" (not running a refresh daily) - which is however how most people use it.


if you switch to an exchange with more pairs and different rate-limits - this additional call per pair can very easily add minutes to the "not 1 call" download case.
It'll be minutes on top of an x hour download - still it's pointless minutes for no good reason.

I'm not sure that's a good tradeoff - as it's based on what you currently encounter (essentially, on your current direct situation).

---

Assuming my assumption about using 3 is correct - we'll **definitely** need tests to cover the above scenarios (1 call is enough, 1 call is not enough, ...) - not just because i don't really trust this implementation - but also to ensure it remains maintainable.

Well, here come some thoughts...

Actually, there is only one doubtful moment with the resulting implementation -- it's a state attribute. It's a member of the Worker class (and should be, as I think, be member of this class since it processes the changes in the state -- Running, Stopped, Reconfig) rather than the Freqtradebot class itself (which now implements the trading business logic). The state member is the only reason why it's passed to the Freqtradebot constructor (because Freqtradebot object may modify the state to Stopped in some conditions) and further to the constructor of the RPCManager class (because RPC object also utilizes the state of the bot). So the dependency is not elegant... I even made it optional in Freqtradebot for simplyfying tests that do not implement changing the state and do not check the state of the bot.

I see the following approaches for the state:
* Leave it as it is. Because it's still quite logical and straight.
* Move initialization of the RPC Manager out of the Freqtradebot up to Worker and then pass the Worker directly to it. In the similar manner as dataprovider is passed to the strategy.
* Implement a separate class for the bot state, make an instance of it a member of Worker and pass that member of the Worker to the RPC Manager and Freqtradebot constructors instead of the Worker.
* Something else to make the dependency between Worker, Freqtradebot and RPC more elegant...

In the tests:
* Should the Worker be created in all cases instead of single Freqtrade without the bot state (mocked or not, whatever)? This would allow to remove back optionality of the Worker argument in the Freqtradebot and RPC Manager constructors...

@xmatthias pls review this, thanks.

What about making the state a global var in the Worker module?

Then in RPC and in freqtradebot.py we could use it without passing worker instance as a parameter to `__init__()`:
```
from freqtrade.worker import state
```

(Yes, it will controll the state of all workers if someone created more than one worker...)

The name of this var can be `bot_state` or `worker_state` to be less confusing.

P.S. Or even better a Worker class var (static member var)...
```
from freqtrade.worker import Worker
...
    Worker.state = State.STOPPED
```

discussion_timeline.author: hroff-1902
discussion_timeline.body:
Yes, I definitely like this pattern with the bot state as a worker module global var or a class var.
In addition, in order to prevent creation of multiple workers, member functions of the Worker class could simply be made a module functions (a module singleton). "Simple is better than complex..."

Can we'll be needing multiple workers in the future?

discussion_timeline.author: xmatthias
discussion_timeline.body:
Much more likely than having multiple workers is one worker with multiple instances of freqtradebot attached (even though surely not short-term) - so you have one worker controlling multiple instances, and each bot may have a different state (rpc / config is all bot-related, not worker related).

I think you're making `state` way too complicated. 
You need state in the freqtradebot object anyway, since otherwise you'd need to pass worker to RPC, and therefore pass it from worker to freqtradebot and back just because you think it should not be part of the freqtradebot class.

Also, a global variable is something i very much dislike, since i have been thought that as bad programming style, and which may cause problems/bugs since rpc is running in a separate thread.

Think through (or try) my proposal, and you'll see that it'll make the whole PR a lot easier, since it'll also remove the need to pass config to tests as pointed out above.

Side note: i very much like your PR with the worker - but i think about it in levels (worker is the lowest level, freqtradebot the next, and everything else building on top of this ...) - and we should keep the levels seperated so in theory we could exchange worker with a "threaded" worker, or a "whatever else" worker ...
